content: Maternal healthcare services, especially in lowand middle-income countries, must have access to appropriate medications and training in relevant procedures. Healthcare providers, health managers, policymakers, and other stakeholders require up-to-date, evidence-based recommendations to guide clinical policies and practices. This is essential to optimize the quality of care and improve healthcare outcomes. Efforts to prevent and reduce morbidity and mortality during pregnancy and childbirth can significantly address global inequities in maternal and perinatal health. Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, such as pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, are major contributors to severe maternal and neonatal morbidity, long-term disability, and mortality. Globally, these conditions account for approximately 14% of all maternal deaths. Among hypertensive disorders, pre-eclampsia is particularly impactful, being one of the leading causes of maternal and perinatal mortality and morbidity worldwide. The pathogenesis of pre-eclampsia is not fully understood. It is associated with abnormal placentation early in pregnancy, followed by systemic inflammation and progressive endothelial damage. However, there are ongoing controversies regarding its diagnosis, screening, management, and classification of severity. While disturbances in placentation occur early in pregnancy, clinical manifestations such as hypertension and proteinuria typically become evident in the second half of pregnancy, affecting 2–8% of all pregnancies. Pre-eclampsia is generally classified as mild or severe. Severe pre-eclampsia is diagnosed when conditions such as severe hypertension, significant proteinuria, or substantial maternal organ dysfunction are present. In some regions, early onset (before 32–34 weeks of gestation) and fetal morbidity are also used as criteria for classifying pre-eclampsia as severe. The only definitive treatment for pre-eclampsia is the termination of pregnancy or delivery of the fetus and placenta. However, some women may experience a transient worsening of the disease in the postpartum period. Management of pre-eclampsia aims to minimize pregnancy-related complications, avoid unnecessary prematurity, and maximize maternal and infant survival. In 2011, the World Health Organization (WHO) published 22 recommendations for the prevention and treatment of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, including three specific recommendations on managing severe pre-eclampsia before term. These recommendations were developed using WHO guideline development standards, which included synthesizing available research evidence, applying the GRADE methodology, and formulating recommendations through a panel of international experts. In 2017, WHO established a new process for prioritizing and updating maternal and perinatal health recommendations. An Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) systematically prioritized recommendations most urgently needing updates based on new evidence, changes in the evidence base, and factors such as benefits, harms, feasibility, equity, and cost-effectiveness. The GSG identified the three existing WHO recommendations on managing severe pre-eclampsia before term as high-priority for updating due to new, potentially significant evidence. The primary goal of these recommendations is to improve the quality of care and outcomes for pregnant women, particularly concerning the treatment of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. These recommendations provide a foundation for sustainable global implementation of interventions. The target audience for these recommendations includes health professionals responsible for developing national and local health guidelines and protocols, particularly those related to hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. This includes midwives, nurses, general medical practitioners, obstetricians, maternal and child health program managers, and relevant staff in ministries of health. The recommendations are also relevant to professional societies, non-governmental organizations, and implementing partners promoting people-centered maternal care. The recommendations were framed using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) format. The key question addressed was: In women with severe pre-eclampsia before term, does interventionist care compared to expectant management improve maternal or perinatal outcomes? The guideline development process involved six main groups, each with specific roles. The Executive Guideline Steering Group, an independent panel of 14 external experts and stakeholders from six WHO regions, advised on prioritizing new and existing questions in maternal and perinatal health. The WHO Steering Group, comprising WHO staff, managed the updating process, drafted key questions, supervised evidence synthesis, and finalized the guideline document. The Guideline Development Group (GDG), consisting of 16 external experts and stakeholders, appraised evidence, formulated recommendations, and reviewed the final document. The External Review Group, composed of eight technical experts, reviewed the final document for factual accuracy, clarity, and contextual relevance. The systematic review team, supported by the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group, updated the evidence base using the GRADE methodology. The certainty of evidence for each outcome was assessed using the GRADE approach, which rated evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low based on factors such as study design limitations, inconsistency of results, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Evidence profiles were prepared in the form of GRADE tables, summarizing the assessment and judgments for each outcome and estimated risks.
